chapter14_additional_checks: Smaller-background domination requires a semipositive big background, v no less singular than the ordinary-order hypothesis permits, and a strict coefficient below one. Subtraction is performed on common finite truncation levels, never between infinite total masses.
Bounded semipositive-big solvability constructs a density-dependent bounded subsolution; it does not give a uniform positive lower mass for the whole admissible class.
Normalized existence identifies the equation through upper and lower tail envelopes before applying stability. Uniqueness is asserted for the coefficient, not generally for the potential.
One-sided stability bounds sup(v-u)+ from L1 volume error with exponent below (p-1)/(np+p-1), and allows unbounded comparison potentials.

Hermitian Holder regularity combines transform stability, a uniform lower bound for the minimizing radius, and a smoothing-gradient interpolation. Singular-measure regularity also needs domination by a Holder reference.
Local continuity in a degenerate big background is confined to the region where a strict barrier is locally bounded. A power modulus needs the finer regularization error estimate.

Homogeneous replacement in a coordinate ball uses smooth Dirichlet solvability, uniform boundary barriers and translation estimates; its domination property uses upper tests and does not follow from mass comparison.

Contact support for arbitrary big backgrounds permits infinite total mass. The unbounded-obstacle passage controls signed truncation products first, then restricts to the region where the product is positive.

Common-barrier compactness uses a summable self-measure error, rooftops, weighted lower semicontinuity and singular domination. Weak measure convergence additionally requires domination and uniform deep-tail control.

The bounded-subsolution theorem treats vanishing bounded densities relative to a bounded potential measure. Its upper normalization bound uses a nonclosed mixed-density inequality passed from smooth-volume approximants and a fixed-reference trace estimate.

Weighted-measure addition assumes finite weighted input sum. Truncation masses may grow polynomially; exponential self-error still vanishes, and the equation is identified on lower-barrier cutoffs before any global weak-limit assertion.
The relative lower-density lemma bounds the Lq norm from below. It is not a positive lower bound for total mass.

Prescribed positive-exponent existence maximizes weighted mass inside a finite dominating measure, uses the relative type bounds for compactness, and excludes a deficit through weighted addition. The zero-exponent proof keeps coefficient lower bounds and common type bounds separate.

Arbitrary big backgrounds use an analytic strict barrier rather than the semipositive smaller-background construction. Barrier domination works locally off poles and does not require finite total mass.
Varying-reference stability is uniform between a fixed strict barrier and zero. Pairwise Cauchy estimates identify the limit before its density is established by local bounded-product continuity.

Resolved analytic approximants produce equations in an exact semipositive big residual form. Jacobian factors and bounded remainders identify downstairs equations off exceptional sets, then non-pluripolarity extends them.

Local Holder estimates and exponential cluster compactness are confined to the regular locus. Scalar uniqueness alone does not imply potential uniqueness; invariant selection is one criterion, and the later vanishing-exponent theorem gives general selection.

Interior smoothness requires minimal singularities, local Holder continuity, and a smooth positive density on the whole regular locus. Its argument uses a proper barrier gap on the nonsmooth set, exact Dirichlet approximants with polynomial rates, localization to subpower trace growth, C1alpha interpolation, a polynomial Calabi estimate retaining Chern torsion, a nonlinear trace iteration, and elliptic regularity. The argument must remain distinct from the local nonsmooth constant-density examples.

Semipositive degeneration replaces the earlier strict barrier and regular locus by new section data. Constants and solution ranges are uniform; local ellipticity is obtained by a global barrier trace test retaining lowered torsion. Monotone normalizers have a perturbation-independent limit. Closedness supplies the mass identity and energy uniqueness in the nodal example.

Nodal pushforward density has the sharp p<3 integrability range and weak L3 endpoint. Potential descent asserts boundedness, not continuity at nodes. Gromov–Hausdorff convergence needs separate shrinking conditions for approximating tubes and limiting punctured neighborhoods. Small curve area needs a uniform upper metric bound; the fixed-volume surface example separates the two diameter conditions.

The projective selection class is invariant under the group generated by U(2) x U(2) and block exchange. Bounded invariant solutions are reduced through a distributional radial flux, including jump exclusion, before ordinary differential equations and projective end boundedness identify the selected solution.

On the zero-density band the positive-exponent factor changes no radial equation. The slope equals the selected zero-exponent slope, so all these solutions are locally C1,1 and fail C2 at the specified transition hypersurfaces. This does not extend to positive density.

Smooth boundary traces on small coordinate balls identify the bounded solution with the smooth closed Dirichlet solution. Local positivity of the density alone permits discontinuity or a locally Lipschitz non-C1 potential; the compact discontinuity example has a globally L1 density outside every higher Lp class.

Resolved ordinary equations require a strictly positive residual form on a modification. The Jacobian supplies an Lp transported density but can destroy strict positivity upstairs. The normalized solution has Holder remainder upstairs; potential uniqueness and the scalar mass formula require the stated closed or background-power hypotheses.

Minimal blowup equations use an indefinite background pi^*h+c Theta_E; minimal potentials have exactly c L plus bounded target potential. Smooth-center codimension r yields every pushforward Ls exponent strictly below rp/((r-1)p+1), with endpoint and sharpness qualifications retained. Finite iterations give a sufficient exponent with the product of codimensions.

Relative measure representation gives an L1 Radon–Nikodym density in a fixed ordinary type and allows infinite carrier mass. The representing measure is sigma-finite; no bounded density domination follows. The bounded-reference specialization is separate.

Homogeneous Holder-reference existence first approximates a Borel density by continuous densities, then chooses a diagonal of smooth reference measures. A trace bound controls the coefficient above; capacity controls ranges and the coefficient below; two-sided stability identifies a uniform subsequence limit before product passage.

Fixed spherical measures are chosen before the datum or exponent. A genuine Holder reference dominates them; bounded densities give a homogeneous equation with a positive coefficient and a unique bounded positive-exponent equation without a positive lower-mass assumption. The test is sufficient only and does not classify all measures.

Positive lower mass is equivalent to all finite non-pluripolar measure solvability. At zero lower mass an everywhere-positive L1 datum admits no positive scaled subsolution even with an unbounded competitor or infinite mass. Such obstructing densities are L1-dense, while smooth solvable ones are also dense.

The individual threshold is attained as a subsolution by damped monotone upper envelopes, not by continuity of the Monge–Ampere operator under arbitrary L1 convergence. The greatest normalized threshold envelope need not have an exact equation or finite mass. Smooth density comparison tests can miss the threshold even at the level of positivity.

The integrable Gauduchon formula uses all smooth tests. The universal subcritical L^(2n/(2n-1)) coefficient bound allows bounded approximation; monotone truncation reaches the L1 endpoint. A smooth maximizing metric is not asserted for an integrable datum.

Exact product equations use separated factor data. On a closed factor a mass upper bound converts the threshold measure inequality into equality; nonclosed ambient zero lower mass persists. This gives no equation for every ambient integrable datum.

Continuous logarithmic potentials on a curve supply a Sobolev measure trace, a bounded unique positive-exponent equation, and a uniform O(lambda) selection estimate. Product greatestness is proved against arbitrary subsolutions, while zero-exponent potential uniqueness is asserted only in the separated sector.

The full L^n plus root norm is always complete. Its domain is all L^n precisely at positive lower mass; completeness of the root norm alone is instead equivalent to finite upper mass. The closure of bounded roots is characterized by uniform tails over the full Gauduchon family and need not equal the whole root domain.

The all-Borel power-capacity condition on one density, in dimension n>=3, controls the threshold for every dominated density and gives uniform subsequence convergence to an exact finite-mass critical equation. Root tails alone are not used as a general exact-equation theorem.

A bounded continuous logarithmic potential on each fixed Hermitian background gives a density outside every higher Lp class, coefficient one, and a logarithmic root-tail bound. The construction uses a power capacity bound and is distinct from an obstructing zero-threshold L1 density.

A positive threshold supplies a greatest exponential solution at every positive exponent, scalar convergence and total-variation measure convergence. It does not automatically give capacity convergence of normalized potentials. At zero threshold specially matched concentrating product densities still admit solutions at every positive exponent, but all such solutions are unbounded and their masses collapse as the exponent decreases to zero.

Solvable exponents form an upper interval. Positive endpoint attainment is equivalent to a subsequence with supremum bounded below; greatest solutions have right continuity and a left solution limit, with only a countable possible jump set. No actual jump, universal endpoint criterion, or zero-exponent selection is asserted.

Radial selection on a projective factor with k>=2 gives joint capacity and local uniform convergence at arbitrary relative parameter rates. Supremum normalization always selects the exact threshold potential in this family; scalar centering has a finite limit exactly below the first-moment boundary alpha<k/(k+1). The order characterization remains confined to separated potentials.
